data.hypothesis: A repeated 32-byte SSE2 ASCII-skip hybrid may reduce scan-loop overhead relative to the selected parent's 16-byte scan while retaining scalar UTF-8 decoding. This tests a different block granularity, not T1-style whole-buffer validation. Catalog evidence is mixed: the selected 16-byte repeated-scan parent measured 60.43 µs, while a distinct one-way 16-byte SIMD-prefix/scalar-suffix program measured 39.98 µs against the 49.62 µs baseline. Whether 32-byte scans help the official mixed-width n=65536 workload remains unmeasured.

memory_lessons.applicability: Use these results to motivate a contrasting scan strategy, not to predict its speed; the official mixed-width measurement is decisive.
memory_lessons.claim: The T2 catalog reports five distinct valid programs. The one-way 16-byte SIMD-prefix/scalar-suffix program measured 39.98 µs, below the 49.62 µs baseline; the selected repeated-scan parent measured 60.43 µs. Thus an earlier claim that all T2 programs were slower than baseline is contradicted by the recorded measurements.
memory_lessons.next_experiment: Measure this repeated 32-byte scan on the official mixed-width n=65536 workload and run the official ASCII/malformed boundary checks.

data.notes: The 32-byte vector path requires at least 32 remaining bytes and only advances when both vectors are ASCII. On a high bit, it leaves the index at the block boundary; scalar scanning and decoding validate the first high-bit byte, including a stray continuation. The scalar tail remains bounded by length. No performance gain is claimed before controller measurement.
transformations: Changed the repeated ASCII scan from one 16-byte vector per iteration to two adjacent 16-byte vectors checked together; scan only when at least 32 bytes remain.
Skip a 32-byte block only when the OR-combined vectors have no high bits. Otherwise leave the index unchanged for scalar scanning and strict decoding from the known boundary.
Retained bounded scalar tail handling, UTF-8 validity rules, ABI, output, and thread budget.
